final_text:
Here's my read on the three open calls that come closest to Plastic pathways (#2), then who should lead and who to bring in.

## Best fit: #11 Green, circular and resilient harbours

**Why it fits:** The project's core — tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups (#2) — maps directly onto this call's aim of testing and upscaling pollution-reduction solutions in ports and coastal areas under the Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" (#11). Your satellite debris detections and beaching model are exactly the kind of "systemic innovative solution" the call asks for, and the river-mouth-to-beach framing fits its source-to-sea logic.

**The biggest doubt:** #11 is a deployment call, not a research call. It wants demonstration in at least 4 ports across four sea basins, with port authorities and public administrations as partners, and a local implementation strategy for each. Your project is at 35% and the beaching model is still being validated against last summer's surveys — so the proposal would need to be framed around deploying a near-ready tool in real ports, not developing it. That's a stretch, but a workable one.

**The other two, briefly:**
- **#18 Global Ocean Observing System** — your satellite and data-assimilation skills fit its observing-system slots, but it's a €50M infrastructure-scale call focused on GOOS governance, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and biodiversity EOVs. Debris tracking is a side interest at best; you'd be a small cog in a very large machine.
- **#17 Coastal resilience** — shares the coastal setting, but it's about climate resilience and nature-based solutions (floods, erosion, sea-level rise), not pollution tracking. Weakest of the three.

## Who should lead

- **Jonah Whitcombe (#21)** should lead. He's a project member, and his declared interests — marine litter and Lagrangian analysis — are the closest match in the lab to what #11 asks for. He's also the nightly ranking's top profile match for this call.
- **Priya Raman (#22)** should co-lead the technical core: her declared satellite oceanography is the backbone of your debris-detection method, and she's the second-ranked match.
- **You** as PI would anchor the proposal and own the port-authority relationships.
- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#24)** isn't a project member, but his declared circulation and turbulence work is what makes your forecast-currents tracking credible — worth pulling in as a technical contributor.

## Who outside the lab

I have to be honest here: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I can't name specific people or groups outside the lab. What I can say is what the call itself requires, which tells you what to go look for:

- **Port managing authorities and public administrations** in at least 4 ports, one in each of the four basins (Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, Danube incl. Black Sea) — #11 strongly encourages these as partners, and they're a hard requirement for the demonstration sites.
- **Local/regional coastal authorities** in the port communities, for the implementation-strategy work.
- **Industry partners** (e.g., waste-management or port-services companies) to help with the clean-up deployment and upscaling.

If you'd like, I can draft a shortlist of the kinds of institutions to approach per basin, or sketch the consortium structure for the proposal.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#2 — "Depth-Resolved Marine Heatwave Prediction in the Levantine Basin"** (Weerasinghe & Viswakula, 2026).

Why it stands out:

- **It is the only paper in the slate that tackles marine heatwave prediction directly.** The others are adjacent — SST forecasting (#6), general ocean forecasting (#5), or data assimilation methods (#4) — but #2 is about the exact problem your project exists to solve.
- **It is depth-resolved, not just surface.** Most heatwave work stops at sea surface temperature; this one predicts heatwaves at depth using machine learning and explainable AI, which is closer to what an early-warning system needs to be operationally useful.
- **It is new and open.** It entered the slate on 2026-11-10, is still current, and the code and results are available (Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24030956), so you can inspect the method and benchmark against it.

The runner-up worth a look is **#5 — "An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast"** (Zhang et al., *Science Advances*, 2026). It shows an ML system that replaces the entire numerical forecast pipeline and runs directly from heterogeneous observations — a useful architectural reference if you want your early-warning system to be self-contained rather than dependent on a numerical model for initial conditions.

One caveat: Mycelium's reading of #2 is thin (the abstract is essentially a code-release note), so I'd recommend reading the underlying IEEE ICAC 2026 paper in full before treating its method as a benchmark.

#5 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

results.name: corpus_item
results.content:
#6 [paper] VMCF: VMamba–CNN Fusion Network for Sea Surface Temperature Prediction
Authors: Hao Zhan, Xiaoyan Li, Pengfei Lin, Xueming Zhu, Jiuke Wang, Jane You
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213846
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Accurate short-term sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, specifically addressing the limitations of CNN-based methods in capturing global spatiotemporal dependencies and the high computational costs of Transformer-based approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): VMCF (VMamba–CNN Fusion Network), a dual-branch architecture that combines CNNs for local feature extraction with VMamba for efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation, strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): OISST dataset.
Abstract:
Sea surface temperature (SST) exerts a critical influence on diverse physical and biological processes within the marine environment. Nevertheless, accurate short-term SST forecasting still remains challenging. Current deep learning (DL) models have two key limitations: first, the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods fail to capture global spatiotemporal dependencies; second, Transformer-based approaches suffer from relatively high computational costs. To address these issues, this study introduces a VMamba–CNN fusion network (VMCF), a dual-branch architecture designed to effectively characterize the multiscale temporal and spatial variability of SST. The VMCF combines the powerful local feature extraction capability of CNNs with the efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation of VMamba, further strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion. Extensive experiments on the OISST dataset demonstrate significant performance improvements across all evaluation metrics, clearly validating the superiority of VMCF in SST forecasting. Specifically, it achieves root-mean-square error (RMSE) values ranging from 0.17 °C to 0.51 °C across 1–10-day lead times, outperforming five state-of-the-art DL models.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new on its slate and one funding lead.

## Where the project stands
- **Focus:** tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- **Status:** satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
- **Progress:** 35%.
- **Members:** you, Priya Raman, Jonah Whitcombe.
- **Caveat:** the project's state has never been confirmed by its members, so treat the status line as possibly out of date — worth confirming in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers
1. **#9** — *A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter* (Lim & Hong, 2026). The closest match on the slate: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels, validated against field beach records at Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. Directly useful for the beaching-model validation you're doing now.
2. **#10** — *Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model* (Zhang, 2026). Relevant to the forecast-currents side of the project. Note: I could only see its title and metadata — no abstract or method reading was available, so I can't say more than that.
3. **#8** — *Latent-space data assimilation (LSDA)* (Cornelio et al., 2026). Deep-learning data assimilation for feature-based analysis and forecasting; a method you could borrow for fusing your weekly satellite detections with the current forecasts.

The other new papers on the slate (#3, #6, #7, #12) are about diatoms, chlorophyll-a, algal blooms and fish thermal adaptation — not a fit for this project.

## One funding opportunity
**#4 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System…" (Horizon Europe, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16, still open).**
- **What fits:** it funds strengthening ocean observing networks, observing-system experiments, and validation/uptake of innovative observing technologies — your satellite debris detection pipeline and the field-based validation of the beaching model sit squarely in that.
- **Biggest doubt:** the call focuses primarily on areas beyond national jurisdiction and global-scale GOOS gaps (deep sea, polar regions), while Plastic pathways is a coastal, river-to-beach project. The strongest angle would be framing the satellite debris observations as a contribution to a resilient, open observing network with a concrete service for coastal managers.
- **What I couldn't check:** eligibility rules (institution type, consortium requirements, EU participation rules) aren't visible to me — check the call text before committing.

One suggestion: the beaching-model validation against last summer's surveys is the project's current bottleneck, and #9 is a ready-made reference implementation to compare against — worth a close read by Priya or Jonah. I can't change the project itself; if you want to update its status or milestones, that's done in the app.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus the papers and funding opportunity I'd point at.

## Where the project stands

- **Focus:** tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches using forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- **Current status:** satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
- **Progress:** 35%.
- **Members:** you, Priya Raman, Jonah Whitcombe.
- **Caveat:** the project's state has never been confirmed by its members, so the status line above may be out of date — worth confirming in the app if it's stale.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#8 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).** The closest match to the project's core method: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. Directly relevant to the beaching model you're validating against last summer's surveys — the code and aggregated results are public, so it's a useful benchmark and methodological reference.
2. **#12 — "An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast" (Zhang et al., 2026, Science Advances).** WenHai-E2E generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource observations, without relying on a numerical system for initial conditions. Relevant to the "forecast currents" half of the project: if your particle tracking depends on a forecast system, this is a candidate for a faster, cheaper current-field source.
3. **#9 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model" (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo).** A data release of daily analyses from an operational regional ocean forecast system — a potential source of the current fields your Lagrangian tracking needs. Mycelium's reading is thin here (no abstract stored), so treat this as a lead to check rather than a confirmed fit.

The other slate items (#3, #5, #6, #7, #10, #11) are about algal blooms, chlorophyll-a, data assimilation and ocean warming — adjacent to the lab but not to this project's debris-tracking problem.

## One funding opportunity

**#4 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System…" (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01), €50,000,000, deadline 2027-02-16, still open.**

- **What fits:** the call funds strengthening global ocean observing capacity — deploying observation equipment, observing-system experiments, and network optimization — with attention to under-observed regions. The lab's declared profile ("Observing from space: satellite ocean remote sensing"; "Debris pathways: marine litter tracking") and the project's weekly satellite debris detections sit squarely in that space.
- **Biggest doubt:** the call's emphasis is on biodiversity and ecosystem observations, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the deep sea and polar regions, whereas Plastic pathways is a regional, coastal, river-to-beach problem. The debris angle is a stretch against the stated biodiversity focus, and at €50M this is almost certainly a consortium-scale call — the lab's 5 members would need partners to carry it.
- **What I could not check:** eligibility rules (institution type, country, consortium size) aren't in what I can see, so check the call text before committing.

If the biodiversity framing feels too far, the more honest read is that #4 is a *possible* fit for the lab's observing work generally rather than for Plastic pathways specifically — but it's the only open grant on the project's slate, and it's the one worth a closer look.

#12 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

results.name: projects_get
results.content:
#1
Project: Marine heatwave early warning (scope: lab)
Focus statement: A two-to-six-week forecast of marine heatwaves for the regional coast, from an ML-corrected ensemble, delivered to fisheries managers through a public dashboard.
Status: Hindcasts for 2015-2024 beat persistence at four weeks; the public dashboard is in testing with two fisheries offices.
Progress: 60%
Research areas: marine heatwave prediction; ocean data assimilation; ocean data dashboards
Keywords: subseasonal forecasting; sea surface temperature; fisheries
State: never confirmed by its members.
Members: Mara Ellison, Tomás Ferreira-Lind, Sun-hee Park

results.name: projects_get
results.content:
#2
Project: Plastic pathways (scope: lab)
Focus statement: Tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
Status: Satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
Progress: 35%
Research areas: marine litter tracking; satellite ocean remote sensing
Keywords: Lagrangian particle tracking; beaching; floating debris detection
State: never confirmed by its members.
Members: Mara Ellison, Priya Raman, Jonah Whitcombe

Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

IOC-GOOS, constituting the internationally recognised framework for in situ ocean observations worldwide, provides the global backbone for the development and monitoring of Essential Ocean Variables (EOVs),[2] and underpins European capacities such as Copernicus Marine Service and EU-funded research and innovation activities under Horizon Europe. Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.

Evolving geopolitical dynamics and reduced engagement by key international partners pose significant risks to the continuity, openness and resilience of global ocean observing systems, in particular in areas beyond national jurisdictions, highlighting the need for reinforced European action to safeguard scientific sovereignty and long-term, reliable observations and predictions. #60 [grant] Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying land and ocean carbon sources and sinks, reconciling estimates between climate science and national emissions reporting communities, and understanding the drivers (natural and anthropogenic) of these fluxes for accurate climate models and mit…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The text describes a funding call for research projects that must address one of three specific areas: (A) improving understanding and quantification of oceanic CO2 mechanisms under past, present, and future conditions; (B) isolating and quantifying key factors driving land carbon fluxes under curr…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The scope covers global land ecosystems (including inland waters) and the ocean, with a focus on past (including palaeo records), present, and future conditions under various climate change and emission scenarios. It involves coordination between ESA and the European Commission under the Earth Syst…
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. The projects should contribute to a better understanding of the biophysical potential for marine mitigation approaches (in particular carbon dioxide removal) and their implications over relevant timeframes, including feedbacks. The analysis should also include responses to ambitious mitigation (e.g., atmospheric stabilisation in line with policy objectives). Projects should build on the results of related earlier projects, in particular those under call HORIZON-CL6-2022-CLIMATE-01-02.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#29 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

results.content:
#53 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#37 [paper] Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 data using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model
Authors: Abdul Basit, Gabriele Moser, Sebastiano B. Serpico
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3116961
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The non-linear relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) measurements, which varies based on seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hybrid context construction approach combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select historical samples for a transformer-based tabular foundation model (TabICLv2) performing in-context learning.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements from the Ligurian sea, Italy.
Abstract:
Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) concentration is a crucial environmental parameter for monitoring marine and freshwater ecosystems. As a biological indicator, it measures the levels of CHL-a, a green pigment that reflects the presence of phytoplankton in aquatic environments. Remote sensing is a powerful tool for monitoring the spatial distribution of CHL-a concentration. In particular, multispectral data acquired by passive optical sensors can be used to model the relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ CHL-a measurements collected during field visits. However, this relationship is highly non-linear and varies with seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes. This paper proposes a formulation of a tabular foundation model based on a hybrid context construction approach for online CHL-a estimation, combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select informative historical samples. The approach is implemented using a transformer-based tabular foundation model, TabICLv2, which performs prediction through in-context learning. For each query sample, a fixed number of relevant observations are dynamically retrieved and used as contextual input for inference. A dataset comprising time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements of the Ligurian sea, Italy, was constructed. Experiments were performed by comparing both with alternative formulations of TabICLv2 and with traditional machine learning models, including Random Forest (RF) and Adaptive Random Forest (ARF, with a Hoeffding tree as the base learner). While all models benefit from selecting a fixed number of relevant samples, the improvement is more pronounced for TabICLv2, which achieves the best overall performance. These findings highlight the importance of structured context selection and demonstrate the potential of in-context learning for temporally dynamic remote sensing applications.

final_text:
Here's what I found.

---

## Best-fit open grant: #6

**"Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** — Horizon Europe, €3M–€15M, deadline **4 March 2027**, still open.

**Why it fits #1:** The call explicitly asks for AI-based approaches to predict extreme events, seamless prediction from short-term to sub-seasonal scales, and improved early warning systems. Your project is an ML-corrected ensemble producing 2–6 week marine heatwave forecasts delivered to fisheries managers — that is almost a point-for-point match. The call also encourages integration with Copernicus and Destination Earth, which your dashboard delivery model could plug into.

**The biggest doubt:** This is a large consortium call (€3M–€15M, Horizon Europe). You will need partners beyond your lab — at minimum a climate-modelling group and ideally a Copernicus or Destination Earth node. Also, the call's scope is broad (all extreme events, continental to local scale); your project is specifically marine heatwaves, so the proposal would need to frame MHWs as one emblematic case within a wider extremes narrative.

The other open grants I checked are weaker fits:
- **#16** (NSF OTIC) is about instrumentation development, not forecasting — a mismatch with the project's core.
- **#7, #4, #3** are all US SBIR/STTR topics on edge AI, neuromorphic sensing, or subsurface hazard detection — different domains entirely.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and slot analysis point to **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#28)** as the strongest lead:
- He covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models), which is the one slot any lab member covers.
- His declared interests (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML) align with the call's emphasis on model hierarchies and AI-based approaches.
- The ranking places him as the closest profile match (69%).

**You (#24)** are the next closest (67%) and, as PI, would naturally co-lead or be the PI of record. Your declared interests in ocean extremes and data assimilation with ML map directly onto the call's problem statement.

**Sun-hee Park (#27)** (ocean data tools) would be a natural third on the core team, given the dashboard and delivery component.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** extreme events in a changing climate (as a formal research area), digital twins, Copernicus, and Destination Earth. These are the slots you'd need to fill with partners.

---

## Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't name specific people or groups outside the lab. What I can say from the call's requirements is what kinds of partners you'd need:

1. **A climate-modelling / Earth-system group** — to cover the "hierarchy of models" and "digital twins" slots, and to bring the multi-decadal projection angle your project doesn't currently have.
2. **A Copernicus or Destination Earth node** — the call explicitly encourages integration and interoperability with these. A partner already embedded in one of these would close that gap and strengthen the operational uptake story.
3. **A disaster-risk-reduction or climate-adaptation policy group** — the call asks for benefits to EU/national/regional actors and alignment with the EU Preparedness and Adaptation Strategies. Your fisheries-manager delivery model is a good hook, but a policy partner would make it concrete.
4. **A low- to middle-income country partner** — encouraged for capacity building, and automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding.

If you turn on collaborator search in the app, I can look for specific people and groups that match those slots.

---

**Bottom line:** #6 is the clear best fit. Tomás as lead, you as PI, Sun-hee on the data/delivery side, and you'll need to round out the consortium with a climate-modelling group, a Copernicus/DE node, and a policy or LMIC partner before the 4 March 2027 deadline.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of an alternative to CNN-based architectures that maps parameter count to performance, replaces distributed neural layers with interpretable logic similar to standard programming code, and incorporates reliability metrics to identify when an output is unreliable.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): CNN-based image classification evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing against ResNet-18 and larger architectures on CPU and embedded edge hardware.
Abstract:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.

- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Traditional airborne ISR architectures create substantial burdens on bandwidth, processing, storage, power, and personnel by collecting and transmitting large quantities of data even when the observed environment has not changed.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Combining neuromorphic and event-driven sensing with onboard edge intelligence and temporal machine memory to respond primarily to changes within the observed environment.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Airborne ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance) architectures.
Abstract:
Traditional airborne ISR architectures frequently collect and transmit large quantities of data even when little or nothing within the observed environment has changed. This creates substantial burdens on: Communications bandwidth. Processing. Storage. Power. Analysts. Command-and-control systems. Neuromorphic and event-driven sensors offer a fundamentally different sensing architecture in which the system responds primarily to changes within the observed environment.

The desired capability should combine event-driven sensing with onboard edge intelligence and temporal machine memory. Fundamental engineering considerations include: Event-driven/neuromorphic sensor characterization. Low-latency onboard processing. Low power consumption. Detection of operationally relevant changes. Rejection of irrelevant changes caused by lighting, weather, vegetation, shadows, sensor motion, or environmental clutter. Temporal comparison across repeated observations. Persistent representation of previous environmental state. Confidence scoring for detected changes. Autonomous prioritization of significant changes. Ability to cue additional onboard sensors. Generation of compact change products instead of continuous raw-data transmission. Multi-UAS sharing of relevant environmental changes. Open interfaces for integration with aircraft mission systems. Desired change classes may include movement, addition, removal, modification, displacement, construction, damage, altered activity patterns, or other Government-defined changes.

#3 [grant] Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

## Best-fitting open grant: #4 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open calls in the corpus, #4 is the closest to Plastic pathways (#2). The project traces floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections to target clean-ups; #4 funds place-based, people-centred actions that reduce pollution in ports and harbour communities, with a "source-to-sea" logic that matches your river-mouth-to-beach framing. The strongest reason: both are about tracing and acting on pollution in coastal waters, not just measuring it. The biggest doubt: #4 is a Mission-style call — it expects demonstration in at least 4 ports across four sea basins, with port authorities and public bodies as partners, and your project is currently a 35%-complete lab effort with a beaching model still being validated. That's a real scale jump.

The other open calls fit less well:
- **#15 Global Ocean Observing System** — open, but a €50M flagship on GOOS governance and global observation networks; your satellite debris detections could be a component, not the core.
- **#13 Remote sensing + in-situ biodiversity** — your satellite detection method fits, but the call is about biodiversity data integration, not debris.
- **#18 Coastal resilience** — coastal and pollution-adjacent, but centred on climate adaptation (flooding, erosion, sea-level rise), not litter.
- **#7 Plastic recycling biotech** — about recycling complex plastics industrially; a different problem than tracking floating debris.

## Who in the lab should lead

No one's declared profile covers #4's specific slots (port-based pollution solutions, multi-port deployment), so this is a judgment call on research fit, not a clean match:

- **Jonah Whitcombe (#25)** — declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis, which are the core of the project's method. He's the natural lead, and the nightly ranking also puts him as the closest profile match to this call.
- **Priya Raman (#26)** — declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality; she'd be the natural co-lead on the detection and monitoring side.
- You, as PI, would carry the overall proposal; Sun-hee (#27, ocean data tools) could anchor the data-infrastructure part.

## Who outside the lab

I can't name specific people here: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so no outside suggestions are visible to me. What I can say is what #4 structurally requires of a consortium, which tells you who to go find:

- **Port managing authorities / public bodies** — strongly encouraged as partners, and effectively required for the 4-port, 4-basin demonstration.
- **Local harbour communities and stakeholders** — the call is explicitly people-centred.
- **Industry partners** — for the clean-up and deployment side.

If you'd like, I can draft a short partner-search brief (which basins, what roles, what each partner must bring) so you can start reaching out.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#4 [grant] Green, circular and resilient harbours
Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-03
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-21
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need to accelerate the transition of harbours and ports towards sustainability, resilience, and circularity to meet the objectives of the Mission 'Restore our Ocean and Waters' by 2030, specifically addressing pollution, biodiversity loss, and climate-related risks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Testing, deploying, and upscaling systemic innovative solutions through collaborative actions involving port authorities, local stakeholders, scientific, and industry partners; use of pilot ports, living labs, summer schools, twinning, and technical assistance/capacity-building for smaller ports.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Coastal and inland ports and their related communities across four sea and river basins: Atlantic and Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North Sea, and Danube (including Black Sea).
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This topic aims at directly engaging and supporting harbour/ports and their communities in demonstrating and accelerating the transitions needed for achieving one or several objectives of the Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters”. The participation of relevant public bodies managing port authorities and their communities as partners of the consortium is strongly encouraged.

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Measurable, quantifiable, verifiable and ambitious progress towards reaching one or several interlinked objectives and targets of the Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters by 2030”, as set out in the Mission Implementation Plan[1] through implementation of effective and well-managed place-based and people-centred actions;

- Involvement and increased readiness port cities and authorities for testing, deploying and upscaling systemic innovative solutions for restoring ecosystems and preventing their degradation, including by monitoring invasive species brought through maritime traffic or facilitating ecosystem connectivity;

- Increased number of port cities and authorities taking concrete measures to protect and restore marine and freshwater ecosystems and biodiversity, prevent and eliminate pollution of our ocean, seas and waters, and make the blue economy carbon-neutral and circular;

- Increased resilience of port/cities/authorities and their related communities to extreme climate events; sea-level rise and other environmental challenges (floods, droughts, sea-level rise, etc.) through in particular the reduction of pollution and improved environmental management in harbour areas;

Enhanced knowledge sharing across and within ports and their related communities, facilitating scalable and sustainable practices.

Scope:

The goal of this topic is to accelerate the implementation of innovative solutions to achieve Mission objectives and targets in ports in line with existing legislation like the Industrial Emissions Directive[2], the Water Framework Directive[3], the Marine Strategy Framework Directive[4], the Waste Framework Directive[5], the Maritime Spatial Planning Directive[6] , the Nature Restoration Regulation [7] ,the upcoming EU Port Strategy, Industrial Maritime Strategy and the European Ocean Pact [8].

Proposals under this topic should test, deploy, and upscale systemic innovative solutions to improve sustainability and resilience in ports to reduce pollution and environmental degradation, reverse biodiversity loss, and improve natural resource management in port areas. Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty of recycling complex plastic materials (multi-material, multi-layer, and composites) in sectors such as packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure, and transport.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and pilot-scale demonstration of biotech solutions, specifically the application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced plastic degradation, integrated with the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework and lifecycle assessments.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Industrial value chains within the European Union, targeting a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 4-5.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- environment and society at large benefit from recyclable plastic products which can be recycled back into high value applications;

- industrial value chains introduce circular plastic products on the market through enhanced design for recycling and solutions for effective sorting and recycling on a large scale;

- industrial value chains are equipped with improved characterisation of waste from complex plastic materials to enable its recycling.

Scope:

The topic supports the European Green Deal, the Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste, the Waste Shipment Regulation, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, the upcoming Circular Economy Act and contributes to Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products. final_text:
Here's what I found.

## Best-fit open grant: #6 — "Increasing riparian and coastal areas resilience to climate change, including in waterfront cities and islands"

Still open, deadline **2027-09-21**, €1M–€8.9M. It asks for innovative solutions demonstrated in real conditions, using an **integrated source-to-sea approach** and a living-labs format, in one of four EU sea basins (#6).

Why it fits #2 Plastic pathways:
- **The strongest reason:** the call's source-to-sea framing is almost exactly your project's structure — tracing floating debris *from river mouths to beaches* to target clean-ups (#2). Your satellite debris detections and beaching model are the kind of "innovative solution demonstrated in real conditions" the call wants, and the call explicitly lists pollution remediation as an expected ecological function (#6).
- **The biggest doubt:** the call is framed around climate resilience (storm surge, erosion, sea-level rise), not pollution per se. You'd need to frame debris removal as a resilience/pollution-remediation measure, and you'd have to pick one basin and involve public administrations managing those coastal areas (#6).

The other open calls fit much worse: #5 (harbours) and #11 (blue forests) are place/ecosystem-focused; #12 (GOOS) is about the observing system itself, not debris; #8, #3, #9 are recycling/materials value chains; #7 is Antarctic; #4 is ocean energy; #10 is Alaska-only.

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking names **Priya Raman (#16)** as the closest profile match to this call, with **Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** and you (#14) close behind. On declared interests:
- **Jonah** declares *marine litter* and *Lagrangian analysis* — the core of the project's method (#2).
- **Priya** declares *satellite oceanography* and *coastal water quality* — the detection and the pollution-remediation angle the call asks for.

I'd suggest **Jonah as lead** (his declared interests sit closest to the project's actual problem and method) with **Priya co-leading** the satellite-detection and water-quality components. One honest caveat: no one's declared profile explicitly covers the call's "Nature-based Solutions" or "coastal resilience" slots, so the application will need to lean on the project's demonstrated work rather than declared expertise.

## Who outside the lab

I can't name specific people here: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and I found no co-authorship paths to any lab member that run only through people I can see. What I can say from the call itself: #6 *strongly encourages* participation of **public bodies managing coastal areas, public administrations, and island public authorities** — those are the partner types you'd need to recruit, and they're also the slots no one in the lab covers.

One gap worth flagging: two of the project's concepts — *floating debris detection* and *Lagrangian particle tracking* — aren't declared in any member's profile, even though the project does them. If you'd like Mylo to reflect that, you can update your profiles in the app.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty of recycling complex plastic materials (multi-material, multi-layer, and composites) in sectors such as packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure, and transport.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and pilot-scale demonstration of biotech solutions, specifically the application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced plastic degradation, integrated with the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework and lifecycle assessments.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Industrial value chains within the European Union, targeting a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 4-5.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- environment and society at large benefit from recyclable plastic products which can be recycled back into high value applications;

- industrial value chains introduce circular plastic products on the market through enhanced design for recycling and solutions for effective sorting and recycling on a large scale;

- industrial value chains are equipped with improved characterisation of waste from complex plastic materials to enable its recycling.

Scope:

The topic supports the European Green Deal, the Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste, the Waste Shipment Regulation, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, the upcoming Circular Economy Act and contributes to Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products. Proposals should:

- advance novel biotech solutions for recycling of complex plastic materials and products (multi-material/multi-layer/composites), namely in the sectors of packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure and transport;

- propose recommendations towards fit-for-purpose regulatory risk assessments for novel materials and recycling technologies (i.e. hazard identification, methodological updates) and take into account the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework;

- consider the latest solutions in material innovation while developing novel recycling solutions e.g. by application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced degradation of plastics;

- demonstrate the solutions on a pilot scale involving the whole value chain.

Successful proposals are expected to evaluate the feasibility, effectiveness and impact of the demonstrated solutions using robust evaluation methods (including lifecycle assessments such as product environmental footprint, where relevant) and present data and evidence about the economic, environmental and social costs and benefits of the developed solutions.

Industrial value chains are expected to take part in the proposed consortia to enable a demonstration of the proposed solution and involve all relevant stakeholders.

Clustering with other relevant Horizon Europe projects is encouraged.
