Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Increased economically viable and functionally equivalent renewable material and sustainable chemical solutions used in large scale textile applications, including apparel, home and technical textiles;

- A realistic pathway for an absolute reduction of the use of virgin fossil-based materials and chemicals used to produce textile products for the EU market by 2035, contributing to enhance the preservation of human health, biodiversity and ecosystems, whether aquatic or terrestrial ecosystem preservation and emission reduction;

Scope:

Innovative renewable textile fibres and sustainable chemical solutions today face almost insurmountable cost disadvantages compared to extremely cost-competitive and industrially entrenched fibres and chemicals based on virgin fossil resources. Specific emphasis must be placed on resulting final product quality, their durability and functionality to avoid negative user/consumer perception of products made with renewable materials and sustainable chemicals. As not all cost and quality challenges may be immediately overcome by technological innovation, accompanying business models and systems approaches are needed to enable equitable cost and risk sharing among all involved stakeholders in the textile value chain.

- Quantification of biodiversity outcomes associated to new processes by using existing Monitoring, Reporting and Validation (MRV) methodologies, adapting and testing them if needed;

- Characterisation, quality assurance and mitigation strategies for the most common processing and functionality challenges and limitations of the sustainable materials and chemicals targeted;

- Development of best practices and training materials targeted at designers, manufacturers, brands, end of life managers and end users, working with the targeted materials and chemicals;

- Strategies and tools to practically implement collective risk sharing and smart scaling approaches.

Proposals should actively involve suppliers of renewable materials and sustainable chemicals, brands, commercial end users and developers/manufacturers of relevant processing technology and industrial partners with the capacity to commercially scale up production with the targeted materials and chemicals. Proposals should carry out research and innovation to develop missing elements and achieve the necessary integration, including economic viability. final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

## Best fit: #7 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open grants I checked, #7 is the closest to Plastic pathways (#2). The project traces floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups — and #7 asks for exactly that kind of work: testing, deploying and upscaling pollution-reduction solutions in ports and coastal areas, with strong involvement of port authorities and local stakeholders, across at least four ports in four EU sea basins. It's open, with a deadline of 2027-09-21 and €1,000,000–€8,925,000.

The biggest doubt: the call is place-based and port-centric, while your project is currently river-mouth-to-beach. You'd need to frame the debris work as a harbour/port pollution solution and line up port authorities as partners.

The other open grants fit much less well:
- **#5 Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center** (US NIEHS U24, deadline 2026-12-01) — about standardizing micro/nanoplastics *health-effects* research; a coordination center, not a pathways project.
- **#4 ZEWT Partnership** (deadline 2027-04-14) — about pollution from *waterborne transport and zero-carbon fuel spills*, not debris.
- **#3, #8, #10, #12** — recycling/circularity of plastic materials, textiles, footwear, electronics; **#9** is the seafood supply chain; **#6** is subsea power; **#11** is air quality. None match.

## Who in the lab should lead

No one's declared profile covers #7's requirement slots directly, so this is a judgment call on who the work sits closest to:

- **Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** — declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis, which is the core of the project's method. He's the natural scientific lead.
- **Priya Raman (#16)** — declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality; she'd carry the satellite-detection and water-quality side.
- **You (#14)** — as PI you'd own the proposal and the port-authority relationships, with Sun-hee (#17) on the data-tools/dashboards angle the call's "tools for managers" flavour invites.

My suggestion: you lead the application, with Jonah as the scientific lead on the debris-tracking work and Priya on the satellite component.

## Who outside the lab

I can't name specific people here — collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so no external suggestions are visible to me. What I can say from the call itself: #7 strongly encourages **public bodies managing port authorities and their communities** as consortium partners, and requires demonstration in at least four ports across the Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, and Danube basins. So your natural partners are port authorities and coastal-management bodies in those basins, plus industry and scientific partners — you'd need to identify and approach them yourselves.

One thing I couldn't check: the full eligibility rules of #7 (institution type, consortium size, country requirements) aren't in what I read, so it's worth verifying those in the call text before committing.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#6 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Measurable improvements in the competitiveness and increased environmental sustainability of the EU’s fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors by integrating circular economy principles;

- Minimized and better managed waste products derived from fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors as well as improved reutilization and reduction of by-products;

- Reduced existing barriers preventing the implementation and development of circular principles in seafood chains, such as the cost of advanced processing technologies, regulatory hurdles, lack of collaboration across the different seafood supply chain actors or limited market demand and acceptance;

Scope:

Proposals under this topic are expected to show how activities and results will contribute to achieve Mission objective 2 - prevent and eliminate pollution of marine and freshwaters and Mission objective 3 – Sustainable, carbon-neutral and circular blue economy.

The goal is to improve the competitiveness of the European seafood industry along the value chain while ensuring optimal resource use and minimising environmental impacts by applying circular economy principles to the aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors.

In this topic, seafood covers marine or freshwater edible organisms, including seaweeds and algae.

Projects under this topic are relevant to the Circular Economy Action Plan, the EU Bioeconomy Strategy, the EU Algae Initiative, the EU Action Plan Towards Zero Pollution, the European Ocean Pact and the Mission objective of making the blue economy sustainable.

The circular approach in seafood supply chain can be applied by the reduction and better management of waste products and/or by improving the valorisation of fisheries and aquaculture by-products which can be used as input for other industries. The aquaculture sector can also explore more sustainable and circular practices as following the example of the Integral Multi-tropic Aquaculture (IMTA) or the diversification to lower trophic species. Another example is the use of innovative organic feed from fisheries bycatch, agriculture products or low-trophic species, as alternatives to traditional fish meal and fish oil, which will reduce dependency on wild fish stocks.

Proposals under this topic should test and demonstrate the technical feasibility, the economic viability and the effectiveness of innovative solutions that improve the circularity and the sustainability of the seafood chain of aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors. #10 [grant] Innovative circular solutions for end-of-life footwear through collection, sorting and recycling
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-05
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current air quality models have limitations in grid resolution and the ability to capture complex interactions between different spatial and temporal scales, leading to uncertainties in assessing and predicting air quality.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a chain of innovative integrated multi-scale modelling systems, including two-way nesting capabilities, improved urban canopy parameterization, and micro-scale modelling systems at very high resolution. The approach also involves integrating temporal scales and indoor emissions, harm…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European Union policy context, targeting public authorities, EU policy-makers, and the EEA. The modelling aims to cover regional to street-level (micro-scale) areas and various time periods.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following outcomes:

- public authorities obtain access to enhanced and innovative modelling capabilities to support air quality planning at various policy levels in a coherent way;

- society benefits from improved governance processes and effective air quality planning strategies, aiming at mitigating air pollution and reducing population exposure, as well as from far more targeted air pollution alerts;

- public authorities, including EU policy-makers and the EEA, receive faster, more comprehensive scientific evidence and tools, enabling more effective EU air quality policy implementation and providing citizens with reliable, detailed information and peak pollution warnings to reduce health impacts.

Scope:

The air we breathe is often polluted, which can lead to serious health problems and even premature death. To address this public health issue, it is essential to understand how pollutants move and interact in the air at different scales, from regional to street level and at different time periods during the day or in different seasons. However, current models used to predict air quality have limitations, particularly in terms of their grid resolution levels and their limited ability to accurately capture the complex interactions between different scales. This can lead to uncertainties and inaccuracies in assessing and predicting air quality, making it challenging to develop and take effective measures to improve air quality.

This topic aims to improve these capabilities by developing a chain of innovative integrated models, relatively easy to use and interpret, that can simulate the air quality situation in different scales and types of areas, including at ‘micro-scale’, and by integrating a temporal-scale dimension, also taking into account emissions into the ambient atmosphere from indoor environments. This should support the development of effective air quality planning strategies at various levels, ultimately helping to reduce air pollution and protect public health. Moreover, it should support the requirements in the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive as regards the development of Air Quality Roadmaps and Air Quality Plans, and for the design and planning of the network of monitoring stations.

More specifically, proposals should:

- develop comprehensive multi-scale modelling chains possibly with two-way nesting capabilities (TRL 5), addressing air quality assessment, including spatial and temporal representativeness, and atmospheric processes of air pollution. Incorporate and improve urban canopy parameterization to better account for complex interactions between urban structures and air pollutants, including the role of urban vegetation in mitigating and/or fostering the formation and/or accumulation of specific air pollutants, with an emphasis on air pollutants with the highest health impacts;

- analyse the current limitations associated with the integration of different models and multiple spatial/ temporal scales in a single modelling system and develop methods to improve and integrate the existing air quality models and required input datasets (TRL 5);

- develop, configure and validate innovative micro-scale modelling systems at very high resolution with the aim of modelling and evaluating the impact of air quality measures to minimize, mitigate, and prevent exceedances at hotspot locations (TRL 5);

- provide guidelines for air quality modelling to support decision making to improve air quality at all scales, including by harmonizing different types of models within an integrated system, as well as promoting the use and development of multi-scale online modelling systems.

#12 [grant] Enhancing ecodesign and circularity of consumer electronics
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- material and product manufacturers apply relevant ecodesign, including design for circularity and design for recycling principles in developing and manufacturing products that contribute significantly to EU climate and through reduction of emissions and resource extraction to biodiversity goals, zero pollution, water resilience, circular economy, as well as open strategic autonomy;

- consumers benefit from more sustainable and circular products, i.e. durable, reliable, reusable, reparable, upgradable, recyclable products including increased recycled content.

Scope:

Electrical and electronic equipment continues to be one of the fastest growing waste streams in the EU, with current annual growth rates of 2%. It is estimated that less than 40% of electronic waste is collected in the EU.[1] Value is lost when fully or partially functional products are discarded because they are not reparable, the battery cannot be replaced, the software is no longer supported, or materials incorporated in devices are not recovered.

Increasing recovery of critical raw materials from waste electrical and electronic equipment is a strategic priority to mitigate supply risks. Today, CRM recovery rates are generally low, with increases requiring new recovery processes and interface optimisation with pre-processing to ensure appropriate material flows for efficient recovery are generated.[2]

Proposals should:

- develop, test and demonstrate new or improved ecodesign of consumer electronics, including design for durability, reusability, reparability, disassembly, separability, recyclability, uptake of recycled content. This may include design solutions for the reuse of components and for easier dismantling leading to increased reparability, remanufacturing or recycling with use of solutions and technologies such as active disassembly/debonding materials and adhesives, and design solutions targeting critical and strategic raw materials;

- assess and provide recommendations for mechanisms and incentives to address the trade-offs with costs and innovation limitations and to reward design for circularity and product durability – such as extended guarantees, “second” VAT reduction, or others –, and test and demonstrate new business models such as leasing and product-service-systems, to the extent that they reinforce positive design changes.

Proposed solutions need to be aligned with chemical safety principles (SSbD) and in compliance with relevant legislation such as RoHS. The environmental performance of the proposed solutions in comparison to existing products should be evaluated from a lifecycle perspective using product environmental footprint methodology wherever applicable. Participation of partners from (associated) countries with actual electronics production is encouraged. Participation of SMEs is encouraged. Consumer benefits are at the centre of this topic, and it is vital that the consumer perspective is duly reflected in all activities. The topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and involvement of SSH experts in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related activities.

This topic supports the implementation of the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, in particular with a view to the reparability of small household appliances, the WEEE Directive, contribute to waste prevention, higher circularity and uptake of recyclate, and Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

results.content:
#13 Coastal Ocean Intelligence Lab [coastal-ocean-lab]
Members: 5
Your role: owner
Department: Department of Earth & Ocean Data Science
Statement: We combine ocean models, satellite observations and machine learning to forecast what coastal waters will do next: marine heatwaves, circulation, water quality and where floating debris ends up, and to hand those forecasts to the people who manage the coast.
Profile clusters:
- Forecasting the ocean: ocean data assimilation, machine learning for ocean forecasting, marine heatwave prediction
- Observing from space: satellite ocean remote sensing
- Debris pathways: marine litter tracking
- Tools for coastal managers: ocean data dashboards

final_text:
Here's what I found across both projects.

## The two most urgent deadlines

**1. #24 — NOAA Margaret A. Davidson Graduate Fellowships (National Estuarine Research Reserve System)**
- **Deadline:** 2026-12-07 (21 days)
- **Fits:** *Marine heatwave early warning* — the fellowship supports master's and doctoral students doing research in estuarine science and coastal management, placed at one of 30 national estuarine research reserves to address key coastal management questions.
- **Who in the lab fits:** **Priya Raman** (satellite oceanography, coastal water quality) is the closest match to the estuarine/coastal-management framing. **Mara Ellison** (ocean extremes, data assimilation) is a strong secondary if the application is framed around operational heatwave early warning for coastal communities.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#46** — *Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture* (Kang, Kim & Jeong, 2026, Frontiers in Marine Science). It benchmarks eleven statistical and deep-learning models on five years of hourly in-situ data from 30 coastal stations, demonstrates a 38-hour mean advisory lead time during a real 2024 alert period, and shows calibrated 90% prediction intervals. It directly supports the "operational early warning for coastal managers" angle the fellowship asks for.

**2. #16 — EU Horizon: Data sharing to support AI foundation models in the energy sector**
- **Deadline:** 2026-12-01 (15 days)
- **Fits:** *Plastic pathways* — the call asks for innovative methods for gathering, sharing, and using large datasets to train AI models, with data-governance strategies (federated training, synthetic data, data-space connectors) and real-life pilots. A plastic-pathways project that pools observation-based particle-tracking data across partners and builds a shared, FAIR data foundation for transport modelling maps well onto this.
- **Who in the lab fits:** **Jonah Whitcombe** (marine litter, Lagrangian analysis) is the natural lead for the debris-transport science. **Sun-hee Park** (ocean data tools) is the best fit for the data-governance / infrastructure side of the proposal.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#41** — *Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking* (Bravo et al., 2026, Frontiers in Marine Science). It uses 4,801 observed FMML items from 158 shipboard surveys as initial conditions for ensemble Lagrangian simulations, produces monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps, and ships a web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard with MPA overlays — a concrete example of observation-anchored, shareable, decision-relevant data infrastructure that the call explicitly asks for.

## Caveats

- I couldn't open the project records directly (they weren't visible to me in this conversation), so the project-to-deadline mapping is based on the lab's declared interests, member profiles, and the deadline list itself.
- The #16 call is energy-sector-specific. If the plastic-pathways application isn't framed around energy-relevant data (e.g., offshore wind, shipping emissions, port operations), the fit is weaker. The NOAA fellowship is the tighter, more natural fit of the two.
- Both deadlines are within three weeks. If you want, I can pull the full text of either paper to help draft the application narrative.

#46 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#41 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

#38 [paper] Data-driven enhancement of ocean surface forcing for accurate floating debris transport modelling in the East/Japan Sea
Authors: Hong Thi My Tran, Young Gyu Park, Jun Myoung Choi
Venue: Ocean science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-2533-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Floating debris transport in marginal seas is controlled by a combination of geostrophic currents, wind-driven currents, wave-induced drift, and direct wind forcing, but the relative importance of these processes remains difficult to quantify without in-situ trajectory observations. This study evaluates near-surface forcing combinations for particle tracking in the East/Japan Sea using 33 GPS-tracked surface drifters deployed off the Korean coast in November 2021. The drifters revealed a clear cross-basin transport pathway toward the Japanese coastline and an early bifurcation near a hyperbolic-type Lagrangian structure. We used a particle tracking model to test combinations of geostrophic current, Ekman current, Stokes drift, and windage against the observed drifter trajectories using MAE and NCLS metrics. For undrogued DX drifters, the best performance was obtained by combining geostrophic current, Stokes drift, and windage. For drogued DO drifters, which sampled a deeper effective depth, the inclusion of all four forcing components provided the best agreement with observations. The optimized forcing combinations outperformed benchmark simulations driven by the GOFS analysis and GLORYS reanalysis in this specific event, primarily because they better reproduced the Lagrangian structure associated with the early trajectory bifurcation. Seasonal simulations showed that winter winds enhance eastward transport and beaching along Japan, whereas weaker summer winds allow mesoscale eddies to broaden particle dispersion. The present framework represents the fluid-dynamical component of near-surface particle transport and does not explicitly include plastic-specific fate processes such as fragmentation, biofouling-induced buoyancy changes, aggregation, settling, or resuspension.

#39 [paper] Coherent eddies redistribute microplastics across the water column
Authors: Álvaro Cubas, Eugenio Fraile-Nuez, Francisco Beron-Vera, Ana Molina-Rodríguez, Francisco Machín, Daura Vega-Moreno
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-60846-7
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The ocean interior is emerging as a hidden reservoir of microplastics, yet the mechanisms governing their accumulation below the surface remain poorly understood. Despite growing interest in microplastic distribution throughout the ocean, in-situ observations within smaller-scale oceanographic features such as mesoscale eddies and fronts remain sparse. Here we present in-situ observations of microplastic distributions from 50 to 1200 m within two coherent mesoscale eddies south of the Canary Islands, an anticyclone and a cyclone. Combining physical oceanographic measurements and microplastic sampling with Lagrangian Coherent Structure (LCS) analyses, we show that both eddies enhanced microplastic concentrations in the upper 200 m by up to threefold relative to regional background waters. Small fragments (< 200 μm) dominated microplastic abundances, while fibers were significantly more abundant in the cyclone and larger fragments prevailed in the anticyclonic eddy. These findings reinforce that coherent eddies act as dynamic drivers of microplastic redistribution in the Atlantic Ocean, emphasizing the role of particle-specific inertial dynamics in shaping the fate of plastics throughout the water column.

#37 [paper] Three-dimensional circulation controls on pollutant retention and mucilage accumulation in the sea of Marmara: A Lagrangian perspective.
Authors: Saeed Hariri, Negin Delsouz Khaki, Tülay Çokacar, Hüsne Altıok, Masoud Rostami
Venue: Marine Pollution Bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpolbul.2026.120444
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Insufficient resolution of physical mechanisms controlling transport, accumulation, and persistence of pollutants and organic matter in the Sea of Marmara, a basin experiencing severe pollution and mucilage outbreaks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): High-resolution Lagrangian particle-tracking framework forced by the Coastal and Regional Ocean COmmunity model (CROCO), comparing ensembles of two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) simulations to quantify transport pathways and transit times.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Sea of Marmara, a strongly stratified, semi-enclosed basin.
Abstract:
The Sea of Marmara is undergoing a severe marine pollution crisis driven by chronic nutrient enrichment and recurrent mucilage outbreaks. The physical mechanisms controlling transport, accumulation and persistence of pollutants and organic matter remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we quantify how three-dimensional (3D) circulation regulates dispersal and retention in this strongly stratified, semi-enclosed basin. A high-resolution Lagrangian particle-tracking framework forced by the Coastal and Regional Ocean COmmunity model (CROCO) resolves transport pathways and transit times, with particles as proxies for nutrients and suspended organic matter. Comparing ensembles of two-dimensional (2D) and 3D simulations shows that vertical processes, including shear dispersion and episodic subduction, substantially modify particle pathways and delay horizontal transport. In stratified sub-basins, 3D dynamics extend transit times by up to 100 days relative to 2D estimates, so neglecting vertical exchange systematically underestimates how long material is retained. A persistent retention hotspot emerges in the southwestern basin, where mean transit times exceed 250 days. Such conditions favour the prolonged accumulation of suspended organic material, although mucilage formation additionally involves biological and biogeochemical processes that passive particles do not represent. Lagrangian probability density functions show that dispersal converges on persistent retention areas that recur across release years and release regions, while the rate of accumulation varies between years. These results establish a mechanistic link between 3D circulation and the spatial organization of pollution retention, with implications for monitoring design and mitigation in the Sea of Marmara and analogous stratified semi-enclosed seas.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#19 [grant] Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13112
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current water quality testing kits for expeditionary forces are too cumbersome, complex, and slow, often requiring chemical reagents, extensive training, and external laboratory confirmation, which creates logistics burdens or health risks in contested environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of new sensors and/or methodologies to improve field kits, focusing on reducing size, weight, testing time, and complexity while eliminating liquid chemical reagents.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Expeditionary, austere, and contested environments involving small, distributed Stand-in Forces (squad- and platoon-level).
Abstract:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

#19 [grant] Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13112
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current water quality testing kits for expeditionary forces are too cumbersome, complex, and slow, often requiring chemical reagents, extensive training, and external laboratory confirmation, which creates logistics burdens or health risks in contested environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of new sensors and/or methodologies to improve field kits, focusing on reducing size, weight, testing time, and complexity while eliminating liquid chemical reagents.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Expeditionary, austere, and contested environments involving small, distributed Stand-in Forces (squad- and platoon-level).
Abstract:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

Here's what I found.

## The grant: #11 Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (NSF OTIC)

It's the only open grant on the project's slate, and it's still open — deadline **2027-02-15**. OTIC funds **instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science** (#11). That's a real fit, but it's a fit you have to *frame*, not one that falls out of the project as-is:

- The project's core is a 2–6 week ML-corrected ensemble forecast delivered to fisheries managers via a public dashboard (#7). OTIC wants a **technology deliverable with broad applicability**, not a single regional forecast.
- The strongest angle is the **ML-corrected ensemble + public dashboard as a reusable forecasting/assimilation tool** — the kind of "enhances observational, experimental or analytical capabilities of the ocean science research community" thing OTIC names (#11). The dashboard is already in testing with two fisheries offices (#7), which is good evidence of real uptake.
- The gap to close: the project's declared concepts include **sea surface temperature** and **fisheries**, and *neither is declared by any member's profile* (#7 concepts). OTIC reviewers will want the technology story to be crisp, so the lead should be someone whose declared profile actually carries the method.

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking named **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#6)** as the closest profile match (65%), ahead of Sun-hee Park (#5, 63%) and Jonah Whitcombe (#3, 62%). But the evidence tier matters:

- **Tomás (#6)** — declared interests: *Circulation and turbulence, Physics-informed ML*. The physics-informed ML is the method backbone of an ML-corrected ensemble, and it's the closest declared match to the technology story OTIC wants. **He's the natural lead.**
- **Sun-hee Park (#5)** — declared interests: *Ocean data tools*. This is the dashboard/delivery side. She's the natural **co-lead or PI-side partner** for the "tools for coastal managers" half, which is exactly the "broad applicability / capabilities of the research community" language OTIC uses.
- **You (Mara, #2)** — declared interests: *Data assimilation with ML, Ocean extremes*. You carry the data-assimilation and marine-heatwave-prediction concepts that are the scientific core. As PI you'd anchor the proposal, with Tomás leading the method/technology section and Sun-hee the tools/delivery section.

So: **you as PI, Tomás as method lead, Sun-hee as tools/delivery lead.** That covers the project's three declared research areas (marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, ocean data dashboards) with people whose declared profiles actually hold them.

## Who outside the lab to partner with

Collaboration search is turned off on this instance, so I can't pull a ranked partner list. But from the papers already on the project's slate, two external groups are strong, concrete candidates:

- **Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang** — authors of *Ocean-E2E* (#20), a hybrid physics-based + data-driven global MHW forecasting framework with end-to-end neural assimilation, 40-day skill, open-source. This is the closest external work to your ML-corrected ensemble; a partnership here would strengthen the "broad applicability" claim and give you a peer-reviewed, open-source method to build on.
- **Huitae Joo, Byeong-Jun Lim, Hae Kun Jung** — authors of the coastal buoy temperature QC framework (#23), a machine-learning-assisted, physics-guided, event-preserving QC scheme for coastal buoy records. This is directly relevant to the *observation/instrumentation* side OTIC cares about — a partner who can speak to the sensor/data-quality layer of your dashboard.

I'd flag one honest caveat: I can't see co-authorship paths from you to either group through people you can already see, so these are "reach out and propose" partners, not warm introductions. And I haven't been able to confirm either group's current institutional affiliation from what's visible here — worth verifying before you name them in a proposal.

Want me to draft the OTIC framing (problem → method → broad-applicability deliverable) around the dashboard + ML-corrected ensemble, or pull the full text of #20 or #23 to ground the partnership pitch?

#20 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#23 [paper] Separating Sensor-like Anomalies from Regional Oceanographic Events: A Machine-Learning-Assisted, Physics-Guided, Event-Preserving Quality-Control Framework for Coastal Buoy Temperature Records
Authors: Huitae Joo, Byeong-Jun Lim, Hae Kun Jung
Venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse14161462
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Coastal upwelling and typhoon-driven mixing can cool a buoy record by several degrees within hours. Sensor faults do the same. Quality-control schemes that flag anomalies by residual magnitude alone therefore risk discarding real events. We analysed 30 min temperature records from six buoys and three depths off the east coast of Korea, spanning 2008–2024, and built a machine-learning-assisted, physics-guided, event-preserving quality-control framework that adds new labels without altering any observation or existing flag. Cooling events were catalogued from changes in the observed surface temperature and in the surface-to-bottom temperature difference and classified using three physically interpretable axes: spatial coherence with neighbouring buoys, vertical consistency between layers, and atmospheric forcing from ERA5 and typhoon best-track data. A station-wise ridge prediction model, fitted to the surface layer at five of the six stations, supplied prediction residuals that served only to flag candidates. Residual magnitude separated sensor-like anomalies from regional-event candidates poorly (direction-free AUC 0.52–0.56); upwelling-candidate and typhoon-related events produced residuals as large as those of the sensor-like reference group, or larger. The physical axes showed much stronger internal operational separability, reaching pairwise AUC values up to 1.000 and a multivariate cross-validated mean AUC of 0.987. These values do not represent external validation because the groups were partly defined using the same axes. The framework preserved regional-event candidates while affecting derived monthly means by at most about 0.0005 °C, yet retained event-scale cooling of up to about 8 °C. Prediction residuals are therefore useful for broad anomaly-candidate detection but insufficient for final event classification, which should rely on physically interpretable, multi-station criteria.

final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

## 1. Best-fitting open grant: #6 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open calls I checked, #6 is the closest to Plastic pathways (#2). The strongest reason: the call explicitly asks for solutions that "prevent and eliminate pollution of our ocean, seas and waters" in port areas, and your project's core — satellite debris detection plus a beaching model to target clean-ups — is exactly the kind of monitoring-and-targeting tool it wants deployed and upscaled. The biggest doubt: the call is harbour-centric. It requires demonstration in at least 4 ports, one in each of four basins (Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, Danube), with strong involvement of port authorities. Your project is river-mouth-to-beach, so the proposal would need to be reframed around ports as the pollution sources and the harbours as the places where your detection and beaching tools get tested.

The other open calls I checked fit less well:
- #9 (coastal resilience to climate change) — about NbS, flooding and erosion; pollution is only a side outcome.
- #7 (carbon sources and sinks) — a different science entirely.
- #8 (seafood circularity) — about the seafood value chain, not debris.
- #22 (Global Ocean Observing System) — a €50M infrastructure call focused on areas beyond national jurisdiction; your satellite work could feed it, but it's not a project-shaped fit.
- #20 and #25 (US SBIR/STTR) — sensor and drone hardware topics, not your project.

#6 is open, with a deadline of 2027-09-21 and €1M–€8.9M.

## 2. Who in the lab should lead

I checked the lab's declared profiles against the call's requirement slots, and I have to be honest: **no one's declared profile covers any of the call's slots** (innovative pollution solutions for ports; multi-port deployment). The nightly ranking puts Jonah Whitcombe (#15) closest, then Priya Raman (#16), then you (#14) — but that's profile proximity, not slot coverage.

What the declared interests do show:
- **Jonah (#15)** — declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis. He's the natural scientific lead: the debris-tracking and beaching modelling is his declared territory, and he's a member of the project.
- **Priya (#16)** — declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality. She's the natural lead for the satellite detection component and for the "monitoring effectiveness of solutions" requirement.
- **You (#14)** — as PI you'd be the accountable lead, but your declared interests (data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes) are the least directly on-topic of the three.

My suggestion: you lead the application as PI, with Jonah as the scientific lead on the debris-pathways core and Priya on the satellite monitoring work. The real gap is not scientific — it's institutional: the call strongly encourages (and effectively requires) **port authorities and public administrations as partners**, and no one in the lab has that. That's the first thing to fix before writing.

## 3. Who outside the lab could partner

I have to be plain here: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I can't name specific people or labs outside yours. What I can say from the literature I read:

- The call's required partners are **port authorities and public administrations** in at least four basins. That's the essential external partnership, and it's a matter of your institution's existing port and municipal contacts rather than the research community.
- On the scientific side, the literature points to groups doing closely related work you could approach: the Côte d'Ivoire dispersal/beaching group (Amemou, Cecchi, Penven, Lett — #29, same Lagrangian + CROCO method as your project), the Norwegian coastal plastic distribution group (Brilke, Calovi, Rød, Richter — #28, beaching patterns and targeted clean-up), and the AI ocean-waste tracking community (Singh — #31; Pushkala & Subbulakshmi — #32). I couldn't check introduction paths to them (collaborator search is off), so I can't say whether you already have a chain to any of them.

If you turn collaborator search on in the app, I can re-run this and tell you who outside the lab is reachable and on what evidence.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

#20 [grant] Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13112
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current water quality testing kits for expeditionary forces are too cumbersome, complex, and slow, often requiring chemical reagents, extensive training, and external laboratory confirmation, which creates logistics burdens or health risks in contested environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of new sensors and/or methodologies to improve field kits, focusing on reducing size, weight, testing time, and complexity while eliminating liquid chemical reagents.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Expeditionary, austere, and contested environments involving small, distributed Stand-in Forces (squad- and platoon-level).
Abstract:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.
