#25 [grant] Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13133
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing UAS for marine species monitoring are often prohibitively expensive, lack integrated high-resolution photogrammetry capabilities, or fail to meet specific operational requirements (size, duration, and NDAA compliance) for field-based research.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a prototype compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS integrating a high-resolution flat zoom lens camera with a gimbal, a LiDAR altimeter/range finder (50m+), and a lightweight battery system (<100 Wh).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Small boat-based operations in wet conditions (IP45 rating) with temperatures ranging from -20 to +40 degrees Celsius.
Abstract:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

#29 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#27 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring
Authors: Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls, Leandro Bugoni
Venue: Thalassas An International Journal of Marine Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41208-026-01266-2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#28 [paper] Uncovering regional differences in plastic pollution distribution along the Norwegian coast
Authors: A. Brilke, Martina Calovi, Jan Ketil Rød, Isabel Richter
Venue: International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13762-026-07430-8
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the mechanisms behind coastal plastic accumulation to enable targeted clean-up actions and policy-making.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Linear regression using plastic weight and item count as response variables against physical and socio-environmental explanatory variables.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 446 sampling transects across 170 beaches on Norway’s south-eastern, southern, western, and northern coasts.
Abstract:
Abstract Understanding the mechanisms behind coastal plastic accumulation is crucial for more targeted clean-up actions and policy-making. We used a systematically collected dataset for plastic pollution along the Norwegian coast, added physical and socio-environmental response variables to it, and used linear regression to identify the most important factors that influence plastic accumulation. We used 446 sampling transects on 170 beaches from Norway’s south-eastern, southern, western and northern coasts. Plastic weight and count were chosen as response variables in several linear models, with different explanatory variables included. Although the explained variance in plastic pollution did not lead to any meaningful insights regarding plastic distribution, other insights were gained. Measuring plastic pollution by weight or item count led to different correlations of predictor variables. There were significant regional differences in models, and some predictor variables clearly show different values depending on the region. Furthermore, geographical beaching patterns of different types of plastic debris along the Norwegian coast found in the literature were confirmed. The southern coast had the largest number of plastic items per sampling area, whilst the north displayed fewer but heavier items. Dividing the data by region seems to be desirable, but more samples per region are needed.

#31 [paper] Implementing AI in Ocean Waste Tracking and Management
Authors: MD Millen Singh
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21974811
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine pollution has emerged as a significant environmental challenge, with millions of tons of waste flowing intooceans each year, causing disruptions in marine ecosystems. Traditional methods for monitoring and addressing thispollution are inadequate in dealing with its ineffable complexity. Researchers are thoroughly investigating the potentialof artificial intelligence (AI) as a revolutionary tool for tracking and reducing ocean pollution. This literature reviewexplores the application of cutting-edge technology in tracking and mitigating marine pollution, such as plastic waste,oil spills, and wastewater contamination. A comprehensive review of recent research was performed, concentrating ontechniques that employ advanced technology for the detection, forecasting, and elimination of marine debris. Researchshows that advanced computer vision and machine learning techniques significantly boost the efficiency and precisionof pollution detection, such as recognizing plastic waste through satellite images, and improving clean-up strategies bydirecting collection vessels for maximum effectiveness. Efforts are underway to form partnerships among governmententities, industry players, and academic scholars to advance these data-centric solutions. However, obstacles persist;AI systems typically demand significant amounts of data and are subject to time limitations, and it is essential toconsider the environmental impacts of AI deployment, including energy use and electronic waste. This paper bringstogether current applications, assesses their effectiveness and limitations, and highlights gaps in the existing research.The ability of AI to transform ocean waste management is substantial; however, achieving its complete potentialnecessitates collaboration across disciplines, strict data governance, and thoughtful attention to sustainability in AIresearch.

#32 [paper] Artificial Intelligence in Ocean Clean-Up: Deep Learning Approaches to Marine Litter Detection
Authors: K Poorna Pushkala, P Subbulakshmi
Venue: International Journal of Advanced Science and Computer Applications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.47679/ijasca.v5i2.117
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine litter contamination and its impact on ocean ecosystems and human societies.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A concise overview of impacts, solutions, and causes, including the use of deep learning algorithms to analyze images and video footage from drones or underwater cameras, and debris analysis utilizing publicly available datasets.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Marine environments; analysis of publicly available datasets generated by previous studies.
Abstract:
Marine litter contamination causes a tremendous environmental issue with a high influence on the consequences for ocean ecosystems and human societies. This study offers a concise overview of the impacts, potential solutions, and causes to address this complex problem with Artificial Intelligence. The sources of marine pollution encompass a wide range of human activities, including oil spills, chemical discharges, plastic waste, nutrient runoff, sewage disposal, and atmospheric deposition. These pollutants pose significant threats to marine life, biodiversity, and ecosystem health. While deep learning technologies have shown promise in various environmental applications, including pollution monitoring and management, their direct application to solving marine pollution is limited. Deep learning algorithms can be used to analyze images and video footage from drones or underwater cameras to identify and track plastic pollution. This study additionally provides debris analysis utilizing publicly available datasets generated by a few studies. The several approaches that are being considered can be applied to the creation and efficient management of litter in the future, preserving our ecology. Collaborative efforts between environmental scientists, engineers, and data scientists are crucial to developing robust and effective deep-learning solutions for marine pollution management.

Now I have everything I need. Let me put this together.

Here's what I found:

## Best-fitting open grant

**#29 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** (Horizon Europe, €3M–€15M, deadline 2027-03-04) is the strongest fit for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1).

**Why it fits:**
- The call explicitly asks for "seamless prediction and projection capabilities" across timescales including "sub-seasonal" — which is exactly the 2–6 week forecast window your project targets.
- It welcomes "AI-based approaches" to predict extreme events, matching your ML-corrected ensemble method.
- It calls for "improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events" — your project delivers a public dashboard to fisheries managers, which is a direct early-warning use case.
- It encourages integration with Copernicus and satellite data, aligning with the lab's satellite oceanography cluster.
- The deadline (March 2027) gives you time to build on the current 60% progress and the dashboard testing with two fisheries offices.

**The other open grant on the slate, #5 (NSF OTIC),** is a weaker fit. It focuses on *instrumentation development* with broad applicability to ocean science. Your project is a forecasting and delivery system, not an instrument. The biggest doubt: OTIC wants new hardware or measurement capability, and your project's contribution is a software/ML pipeline and a dashboard.

**What I could not check:** Horizon Europe eligibility rules (EU institution, consortium size, country eligibility). I don't have your institution's EU status or whether you'd need a consortium partner. You'd want to confirm that before committing.

## Who in the lab should lead

The `knowledge_people_for_call` check for #29 returned no declared-profile matches for any lab member — the call's slots (extreme-event prediction, AI-based modelling, early-warning systems, climate resilience) aren't explicitly declared in anyone's profile. But looking at declared interests and project membership:

- **You (Mara Ellison, #13)** — declared interests in "Data assimilation with ML" and "Ocean extremes" (marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting). You're the PI and a project member. Your declared profile covers the core scientific content of the call.
- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#17)** — declared interests in "Circulation and turbulence" and "Physics-informed ML." He's a project member. His ML expertise is relevant to the AI-based modelling the call asks for.
- **Sun-hee Park (#16)** — declared interest in "Ocean data tools." She's a project member. The dashboard and delivery component of the project maps to her declared area.

**My suggestion:** You lead the application as PI, since your declared profile covers both the ocean-extremes and ML-for-data-assimilation pillars of the call, and you own the project. Tomás co-leads the modelling/ML section, and Sun-hee leads the tools-and-delivery section. Priya (#15, satellite oceanography) could contribute the satellite-observations angle, which the call encourages through its Copernicus/ESA coordination.

**Gaps to note:** No one in the lab has a declared profile in "climate resilience" or "disaster risk reduction" — the policy-facing side of the call. You may want a co-PI or partner who can carry that.

## Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't pull a list of people who've consented to be suggested. But from the papers on your project's slate, here are natural scientific partners whose work overlaps directly:

- **Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang** (#25, Ocean-E2E) — they built a hybrid physics/data-driven global MHW forecasting system with end-to-end neural assimilation. Their method is very close to yours (ML-corrected ensemble, subseasonal MHW forecast). A partnership would strengthen the modelling section and add a global-scale perspective to your regional one.
- **Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin** (#3, WenHai-E2E, *Science Advances*) — they built an end-to-end ML global ocean forecast system that runs directly from observations without a numerical model. Their work on replacing the full GOFS pipeline is directly relevant to your ML-corrected ensemble approach.
- **Jemina Stuart-Smith, Tyson Bessell, Alistair Hobday, et al.** (#7, red handfish rescue) — they demonstrated a marine heatwave forecast triggering a real conservation response in Australia. Their work is a strong case study for the "early warning → action" narrative the Horizon call asks for, and they bring the fisheries/conservation management angle.
- **Shujing Zhang, Neil Holbrook, Alex Sen Gupta, et al.** (#6, subsurface MHWs, *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*) — their four-dimensional event-tracking framework for subsurface MHWs complements your surface-focused forecast and adds depth to the "understanding" pillar of the call.

I couldn't check whether any of these people have consented to be contacted or whether there are existing co-authorship paths from your lab to them. You'd want to reach out directly or check for existing collaborations.

**One practical note:** Horizon Europe typically requires a consortium of at least three entities from three different member states (or associated countries). If your institution is in the US, you'd need EU partners. The people above are a starting point for the scientific content, but you'd also need to confirm institutional eligibility.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#25 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#7 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

results.content:
#6 [paper] Vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves
Authors: Shujing Zhang, Neil J. Holbrook, Alex Sen Gupta, Annie Foppert, Zijie Zhao
Venue: npj Climate and Atmospheric Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01592-5
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) are poorly understood due to sparse long-record subsurface observations and a lack of globally consistent characterization frameworks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A four-dimensional event-tracking framework applied to ocean temperature reanalysis data, utilizing depth rescaling and cluster analysis to identify vertical structure types.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean temperature reanalysis data for the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020.
Abstract:
Abstract Subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) represent hidden thermal extremes that can strongly impact marine ecosystems, particularly when they are large-scale and long-lasting. Although they evolve across time and space, their vertical structure and evolution remain poorly understood because of sparse long-record subsurface observations and the limited application of globally consistent frameworks to characterize them. Here we apply a four-dimensional event-tracking framework to ocean temperature reanalysis data to identify and characterize over 500 large-scale subsurface MHWs in the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020. Occurrences are highest in equatorial regions and lowest in the subtropics. The framework captures extensive subsurface expressions of major events, including the northeast Pacific Blob, which penetrated hundreds of metres below the surface, and the Ningaloo Niño, whose subsurface structure extended beyond its traditionally defined surface footprint. Using depth rescaling and cluster analysis, we identify seven recurring vertical structure types, with five significantly associated with El Niño–Southern Oscillation phases. MHWs generally maintain their vertical structure for months to years, with limited propagation across the mixed layer and thermocline. Together, these findings link subsurface MHW evolution to large-scale climate variability and ocean stratification, providing a basis for improved detection and potential predictability.

Now I have a clear picture. Let me put this together.

---

## Best-fitting open grant

**#23 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07) is the strongest match. Here's why:

- **Problem fit:** The call explicitly asks for improved prediction, projection, and attribution of extreme events, with a focus on early warning systems. Your project's core deliverable — a 2-to-6-week ML-corrected ensemble forecast of marine heatwaves delivered to fisheries managers — is exactly the kind of "seamless prediction from short-term to sub-seasonal scales" the call describes.
- **Method fit:** The call welcomes AI-based approaches, digital twins, quantitative intercomparisons, and retrospective analyses. Your project already has 2015–2024 hindcasts that beat persistence at four weeks, a public dashboard in testing with two fisheries offices, and an ML-corrected ensemble — all of which map directly onto the call's expected methods.
- **Scale:** €3M–€15M, deadline **2027-03-04**, still open.
- **Cooperation requirements:** The call encourages cooperation with EU/national/regional actors, Copernicus, Destination Earth, and low-to-middle-income countries. This is where the partner question becomes important.

The other open grant in your project's slate, **#12 (NSF OTIC)**, is a weaker fit: it targets instrumentation development and facility improvements, not forecasting or prediction. The SBIR topics (#19, #22) are defence- or hardware-oriented and don't align with a research-lab early-warning project.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot analysis point to two people:

| Person | Role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (#6) | Closest profile match (69%) | Declared interest in *regional ocean models* — the only lab member who covers the "Earth system models" slot. His physics-informed ML background also maps to the call's "AI-based approaches" and "hierarchy of models" language. |
| **You, Mara** (#2) | Second-closest match (67%) | Declared interests in *data assimilation with ML* and *ocean extremes* — the two core concepts of the project. As PI and project owner, you are the natural lead writer and the person who can speak to the fisheries-manager delivery angle. |

**Recommendation:** You lead the application (as PI and project owner, with the strongest declared fit to the project's core problem), with **Tomás as co-lead** covering the Earth-system-models and physics-informed-ML slots. The remaining gaps — *digital twins*, *Copernicus*, *Destination Earth*, and *extreme events in a changing climate* as a declared concept — are not covered by anyone in the lab. These are the slots your external partners need to fill.

---

## Who outside the lab to partner with

The call explicitly asks for cooperation with EU/national/regional actors, Copernicus, Destination Earth, and low-to-middle-income countries. Based on the papers in your project's slate and the broader corpus, here are the most natural partner candidates:

**1. Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang** (authors of #33, *Ocean-E2E*)
- Built a hybrid physics-based + data-driven global MHW forecasting system with end-to-end neural assimilation, 40-day lead times. This is the closest methodological match to your project's ML-corrected ensemble. They can cover the **AI-based approaches** and **end-to-end assimilation** slots.

**2. Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong** (authors of #32, *Multi-horizon forecasting for South Korean aquaculture*)
- Built an operational marine-heatwave early-warning system for coastal aquaculture in South Korea, with a demonstrated 38-hour advisory lead time. They can cover the **operational early-warning delivery** and **fisheries/aquaculture impact** slots, and they are a natural **low-to-middle-income-country / regional actor** partner.

**3. Alexia Karwat, June-Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, et al.** (authors of #36, *Nature Communications*)
- Demonstrated multi-year predictability of MHWs in coral reef regions using CESM2, ocean-assimilated experiments, and hindcasts. They can cover the **Earth system models** and **multi-year projection** slots, and the coral-reef angle adds the **ecosystem impact / resilience** dimension the call asks for.

**4. Gregory C. Smith, Fabrice Hernández, Charly Régnier, et al.** (authors of #45, *OceanPredict intercomparison*)
- Lead the decade-long OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team. They can cover the **quantitative intercomparison** and **operational verification** slots, and they are a natural bridge to **Copernicus** and the European operational oceanography community.

**5. Luke Parkinson, Matthew Wilson** (authors of #47, *EDDIE digital twin framework*)
- Built an open-source Environmental Digital Twin framework (EDDIE) with operational applications in flood resilience and coastal ecosystem management. They can cover the **digital twin** slot, which is a gap no one in your lab fills.

**6. Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco** (authors of #38, *Adriatic Sea MHW detection*)
- Work on MHW detection and eddy diagnostics in a semi-enclosed coastal basin (Adriatic), with explicit early-warning and climate-resilience framing. They can add a **regional EU case study** and **mesoscale eddy / precursor** expertise.

**7. Linxi Meng, Xiaojing Li, Yunwei Yan** (authors of #30, *Subseasonal MHW forecast skill, tropical Indian Ocean*)
- Work on subseasonal MHW predictability in a tropical region. They can add a **low-to-middle-income-country / tropical** perspective and a **subseasonal forecasting** slot.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. - Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current DNN architectures suffer from 'Black Box' vulnerabilities, excessive computational scaling, lack of transparency, and a dependency on high-cost GPU infrastructure.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of an alternative to CNN-based architectures that maps parameter count to performance, replaces distributed neural layers with interpretable logic similar to standard programming code, and incorporates reliability metrics to identify when an output is unreliable.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): CNN-based image classification evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing against ResNet-18 and larger architectures on CPU and embedded edge hardware.
Abstract:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

#19 [grant] Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

#33 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#32 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#36 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#45 [paper] Near Real-time Evaluation of Operational Oceanographic Predictions: Over a Decade of Intercomparison by Global Ocean Forecasting Centers
Authors: Gregory C. Smith, Fabrice Hernández, Charly Régnier, Saima Aijaz, Alain Caya, Ric Crocker, Marie Drévillon, Yvonnick Le Clainche
Venue: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-25-0185.1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for near real-time evaluation of operational oceanographic predictions to ensure consistency, quality, and understanding of multi-system spread and uncertainty.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Intercomparison of operational analyses and forecasts against common observational datasets.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A decade-long intercomparison project under the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team, including sea ice concentration and 15-m currents datasets.
Abstract:
Abstract Near real-time evaluations of operational predictions are required to ensure consistency and quality of forecasts. When possible, intercomparisons of such predictions against common observational datasets allows a further understanding of multi-system spread and uncertainty in predictions, and sheds light on quality of both numerical prediction and observational datasets. For the physical ocean, an intercomparison of operational analyses and forecasts was put in place in 2012 under the auspices of the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team. With over a decade of experience demonstrating the evolution of the accuracy of operational oceanographic predictions, this valuable dataset provides a community resource to underpin additional studies such as the benchmarking of deep-learning neural-network emulators. Here we highlight the lessons learned and challenges encountered in this activity and describe how the system is evolving from a research effort into an operational verification activity. We also describe two additional datasets that have been added, namely, sea ice concentration and 15-m currents.

#47 [paper] Development of an open-source analytical Digital Twin framework for environmental modelling and management
Authors: Luke Parkinson, Matthew Wilson
Venue: The international archives of the photogrammetry, remote sensing and spatial information sciences/International archives of the photogrammetry, remote sensing and spatial information sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/isprs-archives-l-4-w1-2026-227-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Environmental Digital Twins are dynamic virtual representations of physical environments that support real-time monitoring, scenario modelling, and community decision-making, that hold significant promise for addressing complex environmental challenges. Yet the development of each new system typically requires substantial duplicated engineering effort, and open-source frameworks specifically designed for environmental applications remain scarce. We present the Environmental Digital Data Intelligence Engine (EDDIE), a free and open-source framework (AGPL-3.0) for building environmental Digital Twins, developed at the Geospatial Research Institute Toi Hangarau. EDDIE assembles proven free and open-source geospatial (FOSS4G) components including PostGIS, GeoServer, TerriaJS, and a Python processing stack into a modular, containerised architecture. A plugin-based module system allows domain-specific environmental models to be registered and orchestrated within a shared infrastructure, while OGC-standard service interfaces (WPS, WFS, WMS) ensure interoperability with external tools and other Digital Twin instances. EDDIE underpins three operational applications: the Flood Resilience Digital Twin (FReDT), which automates compound flood inundation modelling under climate change scenarios; the Ōtākaro Digital Twin, an environmental monitoring and modelling platform for the Ōtākaro/Avon River developed with hapū Ngāi Tūāhuriri and Christchurch City Council; and Te Awarua Kai Ora, a community hydrodynamic modelling and story-mapping platform for Te Awarua / Porirua Harbour. We describe the EDDIE architecture, present performance benchmarks for FReDT, and discuss EDDIE’s potential as a reusable community framework for the open environmental Digital Twin ecosystem.

#38 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#41 [paper] LangYa: a large AI model for global ocean forecasting.
Authors: Yang, Nan, Wang, Chong, Zhao, Zimeng, Zhao, Meihua, Zheng, Huiling, Zhang, Bin, Wang, Fan, Li, Xiaofeng
Venue: Science bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42580897/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean forecasting is crucial for both scientific research and societal benefits. Large artificial intelligence (AI)-based models have recently boosted forecasting efficiency and accuracy. However, it remains challenging to develop a comprehensive AI-driven ocean forecasting system capable of integrating cross-spatiotemporal and atmospheric forcing. This study introduces LangYa, a cross-spatiotemporal and atmospheric forcing ocean forecasting system featuring: (1) a large-language-model-based (LLM-based) time embedding to explicitly represent forecast lead times, (2) an asynchronous cross-iterative random sampling strategy to represent the impacts of atmospheric forcing on ocean processes, (3) an ocean self-attention module to enhance network stability and accelerate training convergence, and (4) an adaptive loss function to capture ocean dynamics in the thermocline, at depths ranging from tens of meters to about 300 m. LangYa is trained on 27 years of global ocean data from the Global Ocean Reanalysis and Simulation, version 12 (GLORYS12). Using reanalysis and observational data, compared to existing open-source AI-based forecasting systems and numerical models, LangYa enables a single model to produce forecasts with lead times of 1 to 7 d (1/12°, daily) and achieves 7 d RMSEs below 0.0736 m/s, 0.0701 m/s, 0.4376 ℃, and 0.1302 psu for global currents, temperature, and salinity respectively. These quantitative results indicate that LangYa provides clear advantages in forecast accuracy, lead-time robustness, and stability for global OSV forecasting, demonstrating its potential for real-time operational deployment.

#21 [grant] Integrating Machine Learning with Computational Fluid Dynamics Models of Orally Inhaled Drug Products (U01) Clinical Trials Not Allowed
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/351059
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Bottlenecks in using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), including computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs) and generic inhaler devices.
Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

#23 [grant] RF Spectrum Operations Enhanced with Distributed AI-Assisted Sharing of Knowledge Sharing (RF-DASK)
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13145
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current Electronic Support (ES) systems rely on Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) to detect enemy electronic signals, but modern adversary radar systems using Artificial Intelligence (AI) create complex waveforms that are difficult to identify and characterize using PDWs alone.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of novel machine learning (ML) methods for dynamic and scalable signal representation and compression to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for RF spectrum knowledge sharing and network-level information dissemination.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Radio frequency (RF) spectrum environments involving emitter detection, classification, and geolocation, with implementation constrained by size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements.
Abstract:
Current ES systems are designed to detect enemy electronic signals by extracting Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) from these signals. Modern radar systems used by adversaries increasingly employ Artificial Intelligence (AI) and it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify, characterize, and represent their waveforms using PDWs alone. To deploy effective Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), there is a need to develop novel methods, including machine learning (ML) [1,2] to enable dynamic and scalable data representation and compression methods that represent complex waveforms, which can be efficiently shared with other nodes in the network. The main goal of this project is to develop advanced techniques for dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for radio frequency (RF) spectrum knowledge sharing and support network level information dissemination for emitter detection, classification and geolocation representative of activity segmentation [3]. Operational size, weight and power (SWaP) constraints should be determined to implement the proposed algorithms on hardware platforms and the developed techniques should be evaluated and demonstrated with hardware-in-the-loop experiments in relevant spectrum environments.

#17 [grant] Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13091
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current physical modeling tools, specifically the JANNAF EPSS suite, lack the chemical and physical mechanisms necessary to simultaneously predict at-source UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emissions for dim hypersonic threats.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Enhancing the JANNAF suite infrastructure by adding thermal protection system response characterization, material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models, and molecular band models for UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emission, integrated with Navier-Stokes CFD…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hypersonic configurations (boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions at high Mach numbers across continuum and rarefied altitudes.
Abstract:
To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA’s existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

#8 [grant] Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

#14 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
